children.text: We are delighted to be able to offer you, on our website, the chance to download the whole of Pavol Satko’s novel, set in the period of the Mongol invasion of the territory of the Kingdom of Hungary in the years 1241 and 1242. Good novels set in the territory of present-day Slovakia in the Middle Ages are as scarce as hen’s teeth, and so I trust that the book will interest as many readers as possible, and that perhaps in the future a publisher will also be found who would undertake to bring it out. Read the author’s short introduction to the novel, and at the end you will find a direct link for downloading the book to your PC or tablet.

blocks.alt: Kronika duší: a novel about the Mongol invasion

children.text: The Mongol invasion, as the event that forms the core of the story of my book is called, took place in the years 1241 and 1242. By that time the making of written records was already commonplace in the Kingdom of Hungary. Not only were donation charters written in the royal chancellery, but also agreements, judgments and, of course, diplomatic correspondence, both ecclesiastical and state. The first chronicles were even beginning to appear, and one of them, the so-called Hungarian-Polish Chronicle, came into being just before the invasion at the court of Coloman of Halych. Unfortunately there is no Hungarian chronicle of the Mongol invasion. The sources of information are chiefly two works, Carmen miserabile and Historia Salonitana, which were written by Italian clerics. In the Kingdom of Hungary itself there was no one to describe the causes, the course and the consequences of the Mongol invasion. It is hard to believe, but so it is; perhaps they did not write because it was all too painful. But neither the Kingdom of Hungary of that time nor today’s Slovakia has a comprehensive and extensive work on the Mongol invasion and its consequences. Apart from a few paragraphs in various historical surveys and collective works, the only genuinely historical article is „Vpády Mongolov na Slovensko v roku 1241“ (The Mongol Incursions into Slovakia in 1241) by František Uličný, published in Vojenská história 3/2004.

blocks.text: Nor have I written a historical book about the Mongol invasion, because I am not a historian. I have written something like history-fiction, but even so I have tried to keep to the facts. I assessed and, where necessary, corrected the information in the works of historians. In doing so I used the results of archaeological excavations, new insights about the Mongols and the records of Islamic and Chinese chroniclers. I read 12 GB of authentic sources (which is why Google Translate took on two full-time Latinists), historical books, theses and articles.

On the foundations of what I had learned I built a romantic story. I brought together the fates of historical men, King Béla IV, Sebeš count of Svätý Jur, Achilles and Kosmas counts of Pezinok, and mixed them with fictitious men, the parish priest Peter and the painter Alexei. There are women in my story too. In the first place probably the finest Hungarian queen, Maria Laskarina, but also a nun, an innkeeper and even several women saints, though not in the proportion required by the European Union. There is the sultan of Damascus, the world-conquering Genghis Khan, the Turkish commander Timur, and St Francis of Assisi as well. Is there sex in it? Of course there is sex in a novel. My own „Fifty Shades of Grey“ only fitted into a three-line paragraph, but either way it is a mortal sin. I fitted the historically real cogs and my own invented ones into an 800-year-old mechanism that can be turned and does not creak too much. (It is possible, however, that, deafened and overwhelmed by my own imaginings, I do not hear the harsh creaking.)

Many of the events really did happen exactly as I have described them. Some probably happened more or less like that, because that is how it came out of what I had learned. And a good many of the stories I made up quite shamelessly. Which are which can be told from the 810 notes beneath the text. The action takes place from Bukhara in Central Asia to Šaštín, and from Neštich above Svätý Jur to Jerusalem. Although it deals with the events of the years 1241 to 1243, it contains my insights and views on the historical causes of particular events reaching back as far as the times of Great Moravia, the rise of the Kingdom of Hungary and the crusades.

I have tried to write an „objective“ historical fiction about life in the Kingdom of Hungary of that time. A country that was the homeland of Hungarians, Slavs, Germans, Walloons, Bashkirs, Cumans, Italians and Pechenegs. Roman and Orthodox Christians, Jews and Muslims lived in it. A Kingdom of Hungary that was more multicultural than today’s western metropolises, and the mutual relations between the various communities were not in the least correct in today’s sense of the word. It was an age when profound social changes were taking place, when learning, towns, the mining of metals and the population were all growing. The Kingdom of Hungary was becoming a European power in the space between the Catholic west and the Orthodox east, and the Mongol invasion changed much of this dramatically.

I wanted to write a different chronicle from those of the Italians Rogerius and Thomas of Split, who could not bear Hungarians and Slavs. A genuinely patriotic work from the point of view of a man living beneath the Lesser Carpathians. I know it is an old-fashioned view, but I understand the people of that time as my (our) ancestors, whom their age set before a hard trial. In it they showed cowardice and heroism, stupidity and clear-sightedness, but above all an enormous strength to survive.

I am not a writer, and in Slovak orthography I commit genocide upon the rules in every sentence. The book probably does not even have the right modern format, and its language is almost archaic. I know that to some it may seem strange that a materialist atheist writes like a Pozsony canon in a cellar at Svätý Jur, but I chose the form of telling the story through the people of that time, and they were believing people.

Ah well. It is what it is, and I am grateful to MBW (my beloved wife) that it occurred to her to suggest that I write the book. With her support I spent several years getting to know that age and writing, which gave me joy and sometimes also filled me with a sense of being useful.
One more note. Any criticism, addition or pointing out of errors will be welcome on my part. I am a man who regards polemic and disagreement as the engine of his own instruction.
